title: Cellular Automata
body:
A grid of cells, each in one of finitely many states, all updated **simultaneously** by the
same local rule applied to each cell's neighbourhood. No central control, no memory beyond the
grid itself. Off the main ladder of [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]]: they share the word
with [[Finite Automata]] but are a different idea, and they are here as evidence for the
Church-Turing thesis rather than as a rung.

The interesting part is the mismatch. The rule is trivially simple and entirely local, and the
behaviour is not.

## Conway's Game of Life

Two states (alive, dead) on a 2D grid, each cell looking at its eight neighbours:

```
live cell with 2 or 3 live neighbours  -> lives
live cell with any other count         -> dies
dead cell with exactly 3 live neighbours -> becomes alive
```

That is the entire specification, and it produces stable blocks, oscillators, gliders that
travel across the grid, and glider guns that emit them forever. Life is **Turing complete**:
you can build logic gates out of glider collisions, wire them into a computer, and run any
computation. A four-line rule with no arithmetic in it reaches the top of the
[[Chomsky Hierarchy]].

## Elementary (1D) cellular automata

The version that gets analysed properly. One row of cells, each looking at itself and its two
neighbours. Three binary inputs means eight input patterns, and each maps to one output bit,
so there are $2^8 = 256$ rules, numbered by reading the outputs as a byte.

**Rule 110** is the famous one: also proved Turing complete, and it is about the simplest
system anyone has managed that for. **Rule 30** produces output that passes randomness tests
well enough that Mathematica used it as a [[Random Numbers|random number]] generator, from a
completely deterministic rule.

Wolfram sorts the 256 into four classes: uniform, periodic, chaotic, and complex. The fourth
is where the interesting ones live, right at the boundary between order and chaos.

## Why they matter here

- **Church-Turing evidence.** Yet another formalism, nothing like a tape or like
  [[Lambda Calculus]], that computes exactly the same functions. The thesis holds up because
  everything keeps landing on the same class.
- **Emergence.** Complexity does not require a complicated rule. This is the standard
  counterexample to the intuition that complicated output needs complicated code.
- **Undecidability, again.** Predicting whether a given Life pattern ever dies out is
  [[Undecidability|undecidable]]. Since Life is Turing complete, that question is the halting
  problem in a costume, so the only general way to find out is to run it and wait.
- Von Neumann invented them in the 1940s looking for a self-replicating machine, and did find
  one. Same [[VonNeumann]] as the architecture.

Related in the vault: [[Simulation]], and [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]], which covers Life and
the 1D rules.

## Core Facts to Know

- Cells on a grid, finitely many states, one local rule, all cells updated in parallel.
- The next state depends only on a cell's neighbourhood.
- **Conway's Game of Life** is 2D with two states and the 2/3-neighbour rule.
- Life is **Turing complete**, so cellular automata compute exactly what a [[Turing Machine]] does.
- Elementary 1D automata have $2^8 = 256$ rules.
- **Rule 110** is Turing complete; **Rule 30** is used as a pseudo-random generator.
- Long-term behaviour is undecidable in general.
- The point is emergence: simple local rules producing complex global behaviour.
- Invented by von Neumann to study self-replication.

Added 2026-08-16: the [[Mandelbrot Set]] in [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] is the same story
told with one quadratic instead of a lookup table. Trivial local rule, unbounded global structure,
and undecidable long-term behaviour in both cases.
